claimVerdicts.note: p7: "With each incremental increase in velocity loss protocol (30% > 20% > 10%), moderate increases in B[La] were observed (~1.7-1.9 mmol/L)"; 12 team-sport athletes, 5 sets back squat at ~0.70 m/s. Within-session measure only.
p9 recommends smaller thresholds (e.g., 10%) "when high amounts of neuromuscular and metabolic fatigue are not favourable (e.g., close to competition...)". Correctly framed as author recommendation.
p9: implemented "by asking athletes to note exercise velocity during the warm up and the first repetition of each set".

Verbatim from the abstract, but the discussion (p22) adds that the post-session effect (SMD 0.58) was "much lower" than within-session effects, "suggesting that the rate of post-session recovery might not be as affected". The brief does say the 48 h effect is untested.

p22 says "Moderate GRADE evidence" of lower post-RT mechanical fatigue "as indicated by less jump height loss or less velocity loss against a fixed load (SMD: 0.58)"; claim drops the velocity-loss alternative and the small-effect caveat.
p1 abstract lists micro-dosing and isometric exercise during fixture congestion; 12 practitioners (11 S&C, 1 physio). p7 adds n = 7 discussed isometrics.

Source is hedged ("It could be argued here that a tendency to remove the eccentric stimulus...") and the concern (p7-8) is detraining over 1-4 weeks and hamstring injury risk, not next-match readiness.
Abstract matches; protocol was 10 x 40 m maximal sprints with 3-min rest in amateur male players, prospective case series (Level 4).
Abstract and p9 limitations: "this study should be considered a pilot study due to the limited sample size".

Values are main effects for time pooled across the float and control recovery conditions (p5), and significance at +48 h is not stated; CMJ height was -7% at +48 h. Protocol was 6 x 10 squats starting at 80% 1RM.

p22-23: OPL "can optimise power development in elite athletes concurrently with sport specific-training and matches possibly due to..." and OPL/VBT "may be optimal for sessions with less TUT, shorter session times".

statementIssues.note: "left measurable deficits 48 hours later" is fair for the sprint study but the squat study reports only pooled descriptive % change at +48 h without stated significance.
"No sample is ... female" is not checked for the 32-study meta-analysis of healthy adults or the team-sport power review; state only for the primary studies.
The interview authors' eccentric concern is about multi-week detraining and hamstring injury risk; framing it as a readiness question slightly shifts the source's point.
OPL is not expanded or explained, which reduces usefulness for a coach reading quickly.
A scope/safety statement was moved into coverageGaps by the drafter's post-processing; it is not a coverage gap.

All five leads (inter-limb asymmetry, ACL differential learning case, creatine and sleep deprivation, HRV norms, parasympathetic reactivation) are labeled "Relevant lead" but are not relevant to pre-competition strength-power dosing.

tierNote: Limited is appropriate: no source tests a session 48 h before competition, the residual-fatigue studies use high-volume protocols, and samples are small. No recommendation is given (recommendedDirection is null) and actions are framed as options.
usefulnessNote: Gives a coach usable, honestly labeled levers (about 10% velocity-loss cap, cluster/rest-redistribution sets, keep volume well below the high-volume protocols, count practice sprinting) and is clear that none is tested at 48 h out. It offers no set/rep dose, which the library cannot support.
suggestedDrafterFixes: When quoting an abstract effect, scan the discussion for the authors' own qualification of that effect (e.g. smaller post-session effects) and carry it into the claim.
For time-course results, state whether values are pooled across conditions and whether the late time point was statistically different from baseline.
Limit population statements (none female, none collegiate) to sources whose samples were actually checked.
Do not label leads "Relevant" unless their title or summary matches the question; drop off-topic leads.
Do not move uncited guardrails into coverageGaps; keep scope/safety text in a dedicated field.
Expand acronyms (OPL, VBT) on first use in practitioner-facing text.
